additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 22A: Automated processing and significant decisions
additions.quote: a decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision
additions.why: The two definitions that decide whether the special-category restriction bites at all: 'based solely on automated processing' and 'significant decision' (a legal effect, or a similarly significant one). A control that cannot say which decisions meet both tests cannot be enforced. In force 5 February 2026 (note F1). Paragraph 2 names one factor to weigh, profiling; 'meaningful' is not otherwise defined.

additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
additions.quote: enable the data subject to make representations about such decisions
additions.why: Meeting a condition in Article 22B is not the end of it. Any solely automated significant decision, including one taken on sensitive data under an exception, must come with four safeguards: information, the chance to make representations, human intervention and a way to contest. An exceptions register should record these alongside the condition relied on. In force 5 February 2026.

additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
additions.quote: processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Article 9(1)
additions.why: The statutory checkpoint at which sensitive data in an automated system should be found: an impact assessment is required in particular for large-scale processing of special category data and for systematic and extensive automated evaluation on which significant decisions are based. It is the legal hook for 'every automated decision checked for sensitive data'. Applies where processing is likely to result in a high risk; it does not itself restrict the decision.

additions.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 10: Special categories of personal data and criminal convictions etc data
additions.quote: only if it meets a condition in Part 2 of Schedule 1
additions.why: The link in the chain the brief describes. Article 22B's contract and legal-authority route needs Article 9(2)(g) to apply; this section says Article 9(2)(g) is met in UK law only if a condition in Part 2 of Schedule 1 is met. Without it the phrase 'substantial public interest condition' has no content.

additions.title: Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, Part 2: Substantial public interest conditions
additions.locator: Sch.1 para 5 (policy document) and paras 6-28 (the conditions)
additions.quote: is met only if, when the processing is carried out, the controller has an appropriate policy document in place
additions.why: The conditions themselves, paragraphs 6 to 28, from which the brief's figure of 23 can be counted in the statute, not only in the regulator's draft. Paragraph 5 adds that, unless a condition says otherwise, it is met only if an appropriate policy document is in place when the processing happens: a ready-made test for each entry in an exceptions register. The page lists one outstanding amendment from Northern Ireland legislation of 2022 not yet applied.

additions.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: Explanatory Notes
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and other departments; published by TSO on legislation.gov.uk
additions.quote: prohibits the use of special categories of data for significant decisions based solely on automated processing unless one of two conditions is met
additions.why: The government's own account of what Article 22B does and why. It describes two conditions: explicit consent, or a decision necessary for a contract or required or authorised by law together with a substantial public interest condition. Explanatory Notes are an aid to reading the Act: by their own statement they do not form part of it and have not been endorsed by Parliament. Note that they count two conditions where the regulator's draft guidance lists three.

additions.title: The Data Use and Access Act 2025 (DUAA): what does it mean for organisations?
additions.locator: Summary of what the Act changes, 'Automated decision-making'
additions.quote: This doesn't apply to special category data which is more protected.
additions.why: The regulator's shortest statement of the position, in guidance that is current, not draft: the Act opens up the lawful bases for significant automated decisions, but not for special category data. Updated 19 June 2026 to record that all the data protection provisions are in force. A summary for organisations; it gives no detail on the conditions.

additions.title: Special category data: What are the substantial public interest conditions?
additions.locator: Section 'What substantial public interest conditions are available?' and the table of conditions
additions.quote: The 23 conditions are set out in paragraphs 6 to 28 of Schedule 1 of the DPA 2018
additions.why: Published guidance, not the consultation draft, giving the same figure the brief takes from the draft, with a table showing for each condition whether a substantial public interest must be shown, whether the absence of consent must be justified, and whether a policy document is needed. Carries the banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. It is not written about automated decisions. The year is that of the latest update noted in the guidance; no date appears on this page.

additions.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What about fairness, bias and discrimination?
additions.locator: Sections 'What about special category data, discrimination and automated decision-making?' and 'What if we accidentally infer special category data through our use of AI?'
additions.quote: such approaches will only be lawful if based on a different substantial public interest condition in Schedule 1
additions.why: Draws the line that is easiest to get wrong. Sensitive data may be used to test a system for bias under the equality-monitoring condition, but that condition cannot support a decision about a particular person; a system that takes disability status, say, as an input to a significant decision needs explicit consent or a different condition. Also warns that a model can infer protected characteristics from proxies without the designer intending it. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; written before Articles 22A to 22D.

additions.title: Enabling responsible access to demographic data to make AI systems fairer
additions.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
additions.quote: Inferred demographic data (and in some cases proxy data itself) will likely fall under personal or special categories of data under the UK GDPR
additions.why: A government advisory body making the inference point from the other direction: guessing someone's ethnicity or health to check for bias creates special category data, and sometimes the proxy is itself special category data. A control that looks only for fields labelled sensitive will miss both. Advisory; 2023, before the current rules on automated decisions.

additions.title: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation
additions.why: The EU has gone further than restricting decisions: it bans outright AI systems that sort individuals by their biometric data to infer these sensitive characteristics, with a carve-out for labelling lawfully acquired datasets and for law enforcement. A UK firm can be caught where it supplies such a system in the EU or its output is used there (Article 2 sets the reach). The Commission's copy of the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. EU law; no UK equivalent; health and ethnicity as such are not in the list, which names race.

additions.title: Guidelines on Automated individual decision-making and Profiling for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP251rev.01)
additions.publisher: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (European Commission)
additions.locator: Chapter III, special categories of data (PDF p. 15); Chapter IV.D, Article 22(4) (PDF p. 24)
additions.quote: Profiling can create special category data by inference from data which is not special category data in its own right
additions.why: International comparator. The European regulators' guidance on the rule the UK provision descends from: under EU GDPR Article 22(4), automated decisions involving special category data are allowed only where an Article 22(2) exemption applies and there is explicit consent or a substantial public interest, and profiling can create such data by inference. It shows the UK's inference point is long-standing, not a novelty of the 2026 draft. EU guidance on the EU text, adopted in 2018; not binding in the UK and written before Articles 22A to 22D.

additions.title: A Right to Reasonable Inferences: Re-Thinking Data Protection Law in the Age of Big Data and AI
additions.publisher: Sandra Wachter and Brent Mittelstadt; Columbia Business Law Review, vol. 2019 no. 2
additions.quote: The GDPR also provides insufficient protection against sensitive inferences (Article 9) or remedies to challenge inferences or important decisions based on them (Article 22(3)).
additions.why: The leading academic treatment of the gap the brief calls the usual one. The authors argue that inferences drawn by analytics get weaker protection than the data they are drawn from, and that the law on sensitive data and automated decisions does not close the gap. Published in a law review; analyses the EU GDPR as it stood in 2019, so it predates both the regulator's 2024 position on inferences and the UK's 2026 rules. Only the abstract was read.

additions.title: Blind Justice: Fairness with Encrypted Sensitive Attributes
additions.publisher: Niki Kilbertus, Adrià Gascón, Matt J. Kusner, Michael Veale, Krishna P. Gummadi and Adrian Weller (arXiv; Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 80, 2018)
additions.quote: an outcome-based fair model may be learned, checked, or have its outputs verified and held to account, without users revealing their sensitive attributes
additions.why: Peer-reviewed evidence that the control can be technical, not only a policy. The authors show that a model can be trained and checked for fairness while the sensitive attributes stay encrypted, so the decision system never sees them. Relevant to the level at which controls are 'technically enforced'. A research method presented at a machine learning conference; nothing read shows it in routine commercial use. Only the abstract was read.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/.quote: The first condition is that the decision is based entirely on processing of personal data to which the data subject has given explicit consent.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/202.quote: For Article 22 of the UK GDPR (automated individual decision-making, including profiling) substitute

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026.quote: Provisions of the 2025 Act coming into force on 5th February 2026

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/.quote: data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited

rejected.title: UK GDPR, Article 22D: Further provision about automated decision-making
rejected.reason: Reachable and already used elsewhere in the library. A power to make regulations; whether any have been made was not checked in this pass, so it adds nothing certain here.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. Its text of Article 22B(1) is unchanged, and the regulator's automated decision-making guidance is still a draft (page last updated 31 March 2026; the regulator's own summary of the Act, updated 19 June 2026, says only that it has consulted). Two refinements. (1) The figure of 23 no longer needs to rest on a consultation draft: the regulator's published special category guidance says 'The 23 conditions are set out in paragraphs 6 to 28 of Schedule 1', and the statute can be counted. (2) The Explanatory Notes to the 2025 Act describe Article 22B as having 'two conditions' (consent; or contract or legal authority plus public interest), where the reading list and the regulator's draft speak of three. The brief's own sentence is consistent with both.
